Enterprises will not fully abandon OpenAI or Anthropic. They will aggressively de-risk them. The default enterprise stack will become multi-model: closed U.S. frontier models for the hardest tasks, self-hosted open-weight models for bulk work, and company-owned post-training/RAG/eval layers as the real moat. Chinese open-weight models will win a large share of routine enterprise inference unless the U.S. produces credible, permissive, enterprise-grade open models fast.

That version is harder to dismiss because it matches what is already happening. Reuters reported that Siemens, Renault, Orange, and ChapsVision are already mixing U.S., Chinese, and European models to avoid dependency on any single provider, and that the Anthropic access restrictions exposed the weakness of remotely controlled proprietary AI services.

1. Biggest correction: “ditch” is too blunt — “route around” is the real move

Enterprises are not going to rip out OpenAI and Anthropic everywhere. That would be irrational. GPT and Claude still matter for frontier reasoning, long-horizon agents, coding, legal analysis, science, and high-trust workflows.

The real move is workload segmentation:

Closed frontier models: hardest reasoning, codebase migrations, high-value research, agentic planning, legal edge cases, executive analysis.

Self-hosted open-weight models: internal search, summarization, classification, extraction, customer support drafts, coding autocomplete, document processing, agent sub-tasks, low/medium-risk automation.

Company-owned layer: retrieval, workflow logs, proprietary evals, adapters, tool schemas, user feedback, business ontology, guardrails, routing, monitoring.

So the best thesis is:

OpenAI and Anthropic will remain premium intelligence suppliers. But they will lose default ownership of enterprise AI infrastructure.

That is much sharper.

2. The killer framing: the enterprise AI stack is splitting into “brains” and “sovereignty”

The enterprise buyer no longer wants “one best model.” It wants five things:

Capability — can the model do the work?
Control — can we run it, inspect it, tune it, and keep using it?
Cost predictability — will agentic token burn destroy ROI?
Data posture — who sees prompts, outputs, tool calls, files, feedback, and logs?
Continuity — can a vendor, government, safety team, or export-control order switch it off?

OpenAI and Anthropic are strongest on capability. Chinese open-weight models are strongest on cost/control. Enterprises will buy both, but they will increasingly refuse to let closed labs become the control plane.

Best line:

The model is not the moat. The routing layer, eval layer, data layer, and workflow memory are the moat.

3. Major factual fix: OpenAI and Anthropic do not generally train on business/API data by default

Your draft says enterprises will not trust Anthropic because it can retain data “at any time.” That is emotionally strong, but too broad.

OpenAI says API inputs and outputs may be retained for up to 30 days for service/abuse monitoring, then removed unless legally required; it also says qualifying organizations can request zero data retention for eligible endpoints.  OpenAI also says qualifying organizations can configure business-data retention and opt for zero data retention in the API platform.

Anthropic says that, by default, it does not use inputs or outputs from commercial products such as Claude for Work, Anthropic API, and Claude Gov to train models, unless customers provide feedback/bugs or otherwise opt in.  Anthropic also offers custom data-retention controls for Enterprise plans, with a minimum retention period of 30 days and default indefinite retention unless a custom retention period is set.

So the better attack is not “they steal your data.” It is:

Even when closed-model vendors do not train on enterprise data by default, they still control availability, retention architecture, safety intervention, model behavior, pricing, and roadmap. That is enough reason for enterprises to avoid dependency.

That is the stronger governance argument.

4. The Fable point is real, but use it correctly

The Fable/Mythos incident is the strongest support for your thesis, but it should be framed as availability and control risk, not simply “data theft.”

Anthropic’s own statement says the U.S. government issued an export-control directive requiring Anthropic to suspend access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 by any foreign national, including Anthropic’s own foreign-national employees, and that the practical result was that Anthropic disabled the models for all customers to ensure compliance.

Even more importantly, Anthropic said Fable required 30-day retention of customer data as part of a defense-in-depth strategy to research and mitigate jailbreaks.

That is the enterprise nightmare:

A vendor can change the data-retention posture of a frontier model for safety reasons, then a government can force access restrictions, then the customer’s production workflow breaks.

That is not a moral argument. That is a business-continuity argument.

Best line:

The Fable lesson is not “Anthropic is evil.” The Fable lesson is that rented intelligence can become unavailable, monitored, retained, delayed, or restricted for reasons outside the customer’s control.

5. OpenAI has the same strategic risk now

This is not only an Anthropic issue. OpenAI said GPT-5.6 Sol, Terra, and Luna are initially being released only to a limited group of trusted partners at the U.S. government’s request, before broader availability. OpenAI also said it does not believe this kind of government access process should become the long-term default because it keeps tools from users, developers, enterprises, cyber defenders, and global partners.

That is huge.

Your upgraded thesis should say:

The real enterprise fear is not just vendor lock-in. It is sovereign lock-in: U.S. frontier models are becoming strategic assets whose access can be shaped by Washington.

For European companies, that is existential. Reuters reported that European firms are spreading AI risk across multiple providers after U.S. curbs, and quoted executives emphasizing flexibility, self-hosting, and alternatives that cannot be switched off remotely.

6. Another correction: “there is no reliable American open-source model” is now too broad

This line needs refinement. OpenAI now advertises open-weight reasoning models, gpt-oss-120b and gpt-oss-20b, under Apache 2.0, designed to run locally on desktops, laptops, and data centers.  Meta also released Llama 4 Scout and Maverick as open-weight models, though under Meta’s own community license rather than Apache/MIT.

So do not say:

“There is no American open source model.”

Say:

There is still no universally trusted American open-weight enterprise base model that combines frontier-adjacent performance, permissive licensing, transparent provenance, predictable roadmap, on-prem deployment, indemnity, compliance artifacts, and long-term neutrality.

That is far more defensible.

Also, Europe has Mistral. Mistral Large 3 and the Ministral 3 family were released under Apache 2.0, and Mistral describes Large 3 as a frontier instruction-tuned open-source model with enterprise customization potential.  So the real complaint is not “no Western open models.” It is:

The Western open model ecosystem is fragmented, while China’s open-weight ecosystem has become brutally practical, fast, cheap, permissive, and enterprise-useful.

7. Stronger rewritten version of your post

ENTERPRISE AI IS ABOUT TO ROUTE AROUND OPENAI AND ANTHROPICAmerican and European enterprises are not going to abandon OpenAI and Anthropic completely. They will do something more dangerous to the closed-model business model: they will stop making them the default control layer.The new enterprise stack will be multi-model. Closed U.S. frontier models will handle the hardest reasoning tasks. But routine inference — summarization, extraction, internal search, support automation, coding assistance, document review, agent sub-tasks, and workflow glue — will move to self-hosted open-weight models running on company-controlled GPUs.Chinese models such as Qwen, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, and MiniMax are attractive because they can be downloaded, hosted inside a company’s own cloud or data center, post-trained on proprietary workflows, wrapped in internal guardrails, and routed through enterprise security controls.That changes the buyer psychology. The question is no longer “Which model is smartest?” The question is:Who controls the model, the logs, the data, the safety layer, the routing, the costs, and the shutdown switch?Fable/Mythos made this obvious. Anthropic had to suspend access after a U.S. government directive, and Anthropic itself said Fable required 30-day customer-data retention for jailbreak mitigation.  OpenAI is now also limiting GPT-5.6 preview access to trusted partners at the U.S. government’s request.That is not just “AI safety.” For enterprises, it is vendor-operational risk.The future is not one model. It is a sovereign model mesh: self-hosted open weights for bulk work, closed frontier models for premium reasoning, and company-owned evals/RAG/post-training as the real moat.The cure is not another closed American API. The cure is a reliable, permissive, enterprise-grade Western open model stack with real deployment freedom, compliance artifacts, indemnity, and no remote kill switch.If your AI strategy depends on giving one closed lab your workflows, your logs, your tool traces, your business context, and your production dependency — then calling that “safety” is cope. It is dependency.

That version keeps the edge but fixes the overclaims.

8. The best headline options

Most viral:

Enterprise AI Will Not Be Won by the Smartest Model. It Will Be Won by the Model You Can Control.

More aggressive:

OpenAI and Anthropic Are Becoming Premium APIs, Not Enterprise Infrastructure

Geopolitical:

Chinese Open Models Are Becoming the Escape Hatch From U.S. AI Dependency

Investor-grade:

The AI Spend Reckoning: Enterprises Will Route Bulk Inference Away From Closed Frontier APIs

Policy-grade:

The West Needs an Open-Weight AI Industrial Base Before Enterprises Standardize on Chinese Models

Sharpest one-liner:

Closed frontier models won the demo. Open-weight models may win the deployment.

9. The obscure but crucial point: self-hosting Chinese models solves data exfiltration, not model-origin risk

This is the missing nuance.

A company can say:

“We are running Qwen/DeepSeek/Kimi on our own GPUs. No prompts go to China.”

That may be true. Self-hosting can solve runtime data leakage if there is no telemetry, no external API call, no cloud callback, no remote logging, and no hidden dependency.

But it does not automatically solve:

model provenance risk;

training-data IP contamination;

embedded censorship or political bias;

hidden behaviors under rare prompts;

supply-chain tampering;

weight authenticity;

export-control risk;

future government procurement restrictions;

customer perception risk;

regulatory uncertainty;

inability to get full training-data lineage;
lack of Western legal indemnity.
Australia banned DeepSeek products, applications, and web services from federal government systems and devices under a mandatory security direction.  South Korea’s privacy regulator said DeepSeek temporarily suspended its app service in Korea after concerns about personal data collection, third-party transfers, and transparency.
So the sophisticated version is:
Self-hosting turns the Chinese-model problem from a data-transfer problem into a provenance, assurance, procurement, and geopolitics problem.
That is the sentence serious buyers will understand.
10. The best enterprise architecture: “sovereign model mesh”
The enterprise solution is not “use Chinese models” or “use OpenAI.” It is a sovereign model mesh.
Architecture:
Layer 1 — Model router
Routes each task to the cheapest acceptable model based on sensitivity, accuracy, latency, jurisdiction, and business value.
Layer 2 — Model classes
Use at least four model categories:
U.S. closed frontier: GPT, Claude.

Western open-weight: OpenAI gpt-oss, Llama, Mistral, IBM/Granite-style models.

Chinese open-weight: Qwen, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, MiniMax.

Internal specialist models: fine-tuned small models trained on company workflows.

Layer 3 — Data classification
No model gets data by default. Data is tagged:

public;

internal;

confidential;

regulated;
export-controlled;

customer data;
trade secret;

board/legal privilege;
national-security sensitive.
Layer 4 — Policy routing
Example:
public marketing copy → cheapest open model;

internal docs → self-hosted model;
source code → self-hosted or approved frontier model with zero-retention terms;

legal privileged data → approved private deployment only;
regulated health/finance data → jurisdiction-specific model environment;
strategic M&A or defense data → no external model.
Layer 5 — Company-owned memory
Do not give the model vendor the memory. Keep memory in company systems: vector DB, graph DB, workflow logs, eval traces, tool audit logs, and structured knowledge bases.
Layer 6 — Eval gate
Every model must pass internal evals before deployment: hallucination, instruction following, domain accuracy, data leakage, political bias, refusal behavior, jailbreak resilience, latency, token cost, and output stability.
Best line:
The enterprise moat is not fine-tuning alone. It is the private eval set plus workflow memory plus model router.
11. Your “data moat” point needs upgrading
You wrote:

“They will post train with their own data on top of Chinese models. That’s how they build data moat.”
Correct direction, but incomplete. Most enterprises should not dump raw proprietary data into post-training. That often creates privacy, leakage, forgetting, quality, and governance problems.

The better strategy is:
Use RAG for factual knowledge.
Company documents, policies, contracts, tickets, customer histories, and manuals should usually stay in retrieval systems, not be baked into weights.
Use fine-tuning for behavior.
Fine-tune on preferred formats, tone, workflows, tool-use patterns, reasoning traces, decision trees, and domain-specific procedures.
Use reinforcement/post-training for actions.
Train agents on successful task trajectories, tool-call sequences, escalation decisions, and human feedback.
Use distillation for cost.
Use expensive frontier models to generate high-quality synthetic traces, then train smaller self-hosted models for routine workloads — subject to contractual limits.
Use evals as the crown jewel.
The private benchmark is often more valuable than the fine-tune. It tells you which model is actually good for your business.

Better wording:
The moat is not “our data in their model.” The moat is our workflow corpus, our eval harness, our routing policy, our tool traces, and our ability to swap base models without losing institutional memory.

12. Missing contractual bomb: vendors must be blocked from vertical cloning
Your draft says Anthropic might retain data and then build the same thing in healthcare/legal. The proof burden is high, but the concern is legitimate.

Anthropic has launched Claude for Healthcare and life-sciences capabilities, including HIPAA-ready products and connectors for clinical trials, registries, scientific tools, preprints, and drug-target resources.  Anthropic also has legal-market integrations; Thomson Reuters announced a 2026 partnership connecting Claude with CoCounsel Legal through MCP integration.

So the enterprise fear is:

The model provider is not just a supplier. It can become a competitor in the customer’s vertical.

That should be handled contractually.

Enterprise customers should demand:

no training on customer data by default;

no use of customer prompts/outputs/tool traces to build competing vertical products;

no use of customer metadata for product-market intelligence;
no cross-customer benchmarking without opt-in;

no retention beyond agreed windows;
customer-owned evals cannot be reused;

customer-owned agent workflows cannot be productized;
customer can export logs, prompts, traces, and fine-tunes;

vendor must disclose when a new product competes with customer workflows;
strong deletion and audit rights;

indemnity for IP/data misuse.
Best line:

A “no training” clause is not enough. Enterprises need a no-compete-by-data clause.

13. The missing category: “vendor safety” can become “vendor control”

Safety is real. Frontier models can create cyber, bio, fraud, and abuse risks. But from an enterprise buyer’s perspective, safety systems can also become control systems.

OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 launch describes layered safeguards including real-time checks, account-level signals, differentiated access, monitoring, enforcement, and additional review of risky generations. OpenAI also says it is working with enterprise customers on privacy-preserving detection, customer-operated safety controls, and access calibrated to risk.

That is actually the right direction. The enterprise demand should be:

Move safety controls into customer-governed infrastructure wherever possible.

Not:

“No safety.”

But:

Customer-operated safety, auditable safety, privacy-preserving safety, local policy enforcement, and contractual limits on provider access.
That is the middle ground.
14. The compliance trap: “self-hosted” does not automatically mean compliant
A company cannot simply say:
“We self-hosted Qwen, therefore it is compliant.”
Compliance depends on:
where the model runs;
where logs are stored;
whether weights are authentic;
whether the license permits commercial use;
whether the model is modified significantly;

whether the use case is high-risk under the EU AI Act;

whether personal data is processed;

whether regulated data is involved;

whether the model can explain outputs;

whether human oversight is required;

whether records are retained;

whether the system affects employment, credit, education, healthcare, insurance, migration, justice, or critical infrastructure.

The EU AI Act is fully applicable from 2 August 2026 with exceptions; GPAI obligations became applicable from 2 August 2025, and the Commission’s enforcement powers for GPAI obligations begin on 2 August 2026.  The Commission’s 2026 GPAI guidance says only actors making significant modifications to AI models need to comply as GPAI providers, while minor modifications may not trigger the same obligations.

That matters for post-training. If a European enterprise heavily modifies a Chinese open-weight model, it may create new compliance obligations.

Best line:

Self-hosting solves sovereignty. It does not erase AI Act, GDPR, sectoral, procurement, or model-governance obligations.

15. The real reason Chinese models will win share: not ideology — unit economics

Enterprises care about ROI. Agentic AI burns tokens violently. Reuters reported that token costs are becoming a pressure point as companies move to AI agents, with Orange saying executives would be “obsessed with cost per token” by the end of the year and citing Uber burning through its 2026 token budget in four months.

That is the adoption wedge for Chinese open-weight models.

The pitch is simple:

Why pay frontier API prices for every sub-task when 80% of enterprise AI work is extraction, routing, rewriting, summarization, classification, and tool-calling?

The future stack will look like this:
tiny local model for routing;
small/medium model for extraction;
self-hosted strong open model for internal reasoning;
frontier closed model only when confidence or complexity threshold is crossed;
human review for high-risk outputs.
Best line:
Closed models will become the escalation tier, not the default tier.
16. The “American cure” should be defined precisely
Your line “the cure is a reliable American open source model” is good but incomplete.
The cure is an American sovereign open-weight enterprise stack with:
Apache/MIT-style license — no weird field-of-use ambiguity.

Frontier-adjacent performance — especially coding, tool use, long context, document reasoning.

On-prem and VPC deployment — not just API.

Full fine-tuning rights — LoRA, full-parameter, RL, distillation where allowed.

Model bill of materials — training-data categories, safety methods, benchmark disclosure.

Indemnity — IP, model-output, training-data claims.

Security artifacts — SOC 2, ISO, FedRAMP path, SBOM/MBOM, vulnerability process.

No remote kill switch — once deployed, customer can keep running the model.

Compatibility layer — OpenAI-compatible API, vLLM/SGLang/TensorRT support.

Reference guardrails — optional, auditable, customer-controlled.

Procurement-safe lineage — safe for government, defense, healthcare, finance.

Long-term roadmap — enterprises need continuity, not a one-off weight drop.
OpenAI’s gpt-oss release is important because it offers Apache 2.0 open-weight reasoning models in 120B and 20B sizes.  But the bigger market need is not just weights. It is the whole enterprise assurance package.
Best line:
The West does not need a hobbyist open model. It needs a procurement-grade open model.
17. The China-model risk matrix enterprises should use

Enterprises considering Chinese open-weight models should score them across 12 dimensions:

License — Apache, MIT, custom, commercial restriction?

Weight provenance — official hash, signed release, trusted mirror?

Training-data transparency — known datasets, synthetic data, code sources?

IP risk — distillation allegations, copyrighted-code exposure, license contamination?

Telemetry — any callback, package dependency, cloud endpoint, tokenization call?
Censorship/bias — behavior on geopolitics, Taiwan, Tiananmen, labor, sanctions, human rights.
Security — jailbreak, prompt injection, data leakage, tool misuse.
Regulatory posture — EU AI Act, GDPR, sector rules, government procurement.
Customer acceptability — will clients reject Chinese-origin models?
Supplier continuity — will weights remain available if sanctions escalate?
Operational cost — tokens/sec, GPU memory, quantization, batching, cache.
Fallback path — can the same workflow run on Llama/Mistral/OpenAI/Claude if needed?
Best line:
Do not ask “Chinese or American?” Ask: can this model pass our model-origin, data, legal, security, cost, and fallback tests?
18. What OpenAI and Anthropic should do to avoid losing enterprise infrastructure
They need to stop acting like the model endpoint is the product. Enterprise buyers increasingly want control.

They should offer:

Customer-hosted frontier distillations
Not the top model, but strong private deployable variants.

Guaranteed zero-retention frontier tier
No safety excuse should silently change data posture. If monitoring is required, use customer-operated safety logs or privacy-preserving detection.

Enterprise continuity SLA
If government or safety action blocks access, customers get a migration path, alternative model, or contractual remedy.

Non-compete-by-data covenant
Do not use customer workflows, prompts, outputs, tool traces, or evals to build competing vertical products.

Right to export
Customers can export prompts, outputs, logs, fine-tunes, embeddings, evaluation results, and agent traces.
Customer-controlled safety gateway
Closed labs can provide safety classifiers, but enterprises can run them in their own environment.
Private fine-tune ownership
Fine-tunes must be customer-owned and not pooled into global model improvement.
Model escrow
For critical infrastructure customers, escrow a deployable fallback model if access is suspended.
Transparent retention matrix
Every model SKU should have a simple table: retention, training use, human review, automated review, government-access risk, eligible ZDR, excluded features.
Best line:
Closed labs need to sell trust infrastructure, not just intelligence.
19. What enterprises should do now
The playbook:
Step 1: Inventory all AI usage
Which teams use ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, Gemini, Qwen, DeepSeek, local models, browser extensions, coding agents, and shadow APIs?
Step 2: Classify workloads
Separate low-risk automation from regulated, privileged, customer, source-code, defense, health, finance, and strategic workflows.
Step 3: Build a private eval harness
Create 500–5,000 real internal tasks with expected outputs and risk labels. This becomes your model-selection engine.

量子位听雨上周报道了逯雨鑫 / yuxinlu1 这个故事，我读完停了很久。

他是在美国读 AI 方向研究生的中国留学生，本科数据与商业分析，有 ADHD。用一张 RTX 5090、32GB VRAM、96GB SSD 约 128GB 总资源，跑了 40+ 小时，烧光 Claude Max 20× 套餐，两个 12B GGUF 模型加起来 70 万+ 下载，一度力压智谱 GLM-5.2 拿过 HF Trending #1。

旁边的名字是：智谱 GLM-5.2、百度无限 OCR、Qwen、NVIDIA、Microsoft FastContext。

一个个人账号，挤进了那个位置。

---

我想拎两层意思出来。

**第一层：indie 对大厂的结构性优势。**

逯雨鑫有一句话我觉得是核心：

"大厂发布开源小模型，往往还承担品牌宣传、API 引流等目标；而个人开发者没有这些包袱，反而可以更专注地解决一个具体痛点。"

智谱出 GLM-5.2，要扛品牌 + 引流 https://t.co/Afb6kAhGCi API + 内部 KPI。百度无限 OCR 要展示研发体量、导流智能云。每一个大厂开源模型都在多个目标之间权衡。

yuxinlu1 只问一个问题：能不能让 12B 模型在 coding 和 agentic 场景里本地好用？

他的选择是 Gemma 4-12B 底座，量化到 Q2_K = 4.5GB，8GB 统一内存的 Mac 能跑。这个 SKU 大厂出不来——不是技术做不到，是商业模型不让做。

**第二层：质量 > 数据量。**

V2 的微调数据只有约 1 万条 examples。

教师数据来自 Cursor Composer 2.5 + Fable 5——但每条思维链对应的代码，都得真跑测试通过才留下。Composer 2.5 做错的题，交给 Fable 5 重推，生成新的推理链和正确代码。Fable 5 后来被 OpenAI 下线，他用 Claude Opus 4.8 xhigh 把缺失的 reasoning 一条条补回去。

结果：V2 在 tau2-bench telecom 子集从 baseline 15% 提到 55%，大约 3.5 倍。他自己讲清楚了：本地自测、单一领域、20 个任务，不能跟官方榜直接比，跟 frontier 还有差距。这个坦率本身也是方法论的一部分。

他自己的总结："数据量没有大家想象得那么重要，真正关键的是质量、筛选和验证。"

---

我做 tar-engine 和 tar-engine-mcp 时走的是同一条逻辑。没做"通用 AI 评估平台"——我没有那个 scope。做的是一个具体痛点：AI skill 和 agent 的安全与质量审计。每条规则都对应真实的 failure mode，都跑过验证，都在 production-ready 状态才进去。不堆量，控制得很克制。

这接续了我之前那篇 builder discipline 里的论点：orchestration > model。

yuxinlu1 这个故事在上面加一层：specialization > scale。即使在 model 层本身，大厂的结构性优势也不是绝对的。indie 的窗口在于做大厂不会去做的具体 SKU，不是在 GPU 池里掰手腕。

---

**三个 takeaway：**

第一，indie 在 model 层有结构性优势。大厂要权衡品牌 / 引流 / KPI；indie 没包袱，可以把一个具体痛点做到大厂不会去填的 niche。

第二，数据量不是杠杆，pipeline 设计才是。1 万条加上"真跑测试通过"的过滤，加上错题 recovery 流，把 baseline 性能拉到 3.5 倍。每条数据怎么来、怎么验、错误怎么处理——这套设计是核心 craft。

第三，ship 时就把限制说在前面是方法论，不是事后 disclaimer。逯雨鑫的 model card 直接写清楚测试条件和缺陷。这种坦率是 builder 信誉的复利。

不必做全能。把一个具体问题做到好用。这是 indie 在 model 层的 winning move。

量子位 (by 听雨) covered a story I keep returning to.

逯雨鑫 / yuxinlu1 — a Chinese grad student doing AI research in the US, undergrad in data & business analytics, ADHD — shipped two 12B GGUF models on Hugging Face. 700K+ downloads combined. Hit #1 on HF Trending, above 智谱 GLM-5.2, 百度无限 OCR, Qwen, NVIDIA LocateAnything, Microsoft FastContext.

The setup: Gemma 4-12B base. Reason: "challenge myself + 12B quantizes to Q2_K at 4.5GB, runs on 8GB unified memory Mac." V1 targets coding. V2 targets agentic tasks.

Data pipeline: teacher signals from Cursor Composer 2.5 + Fable 5. Filter rule — every reasoning chain's code had to actually run and pass tests before it stayed. Composer 2.5 errors got re-routed to Fable 5 for fresh reasoning + correct code. When OpenAI took Fable 5 offline mid-build, missing reasoning in community-contributed data got backfilled with Claude Opus 4.8 (xhigh), one entry at a time. Total training data: ~10,000 examples.

V2 result on tau2-bench telecom subset: 15% baseline → 55%. ~3.5x. Single-domain, local self-test, 20 tasks — he states all of this upfront, not buried in footnotes.

Two lines from the interview:

"大厂发布开源小模型, 往往还承担品牌宣传、API 引流等目标; 而个人开发者没有这些包袱, 反而可以更专注地解决一个具体痛点。"

"数据量没有大家想象得那么重要, 真正关键的是质量、筛选和验证。"

Both land hard if you've shipped anything model-adjacent.

When I open-sourced tar-engine + tar-engine-mcp, the same logic held. I didn't build a general AI eval platform — I had no compute budget for that scope. I built one specific thing: security and quality auditing for AI skills and agents. Every rule maps to a real failure mode, runs against a baseline skill set, ships only when it's production-ready. No rule added just to inflate coverage.

That's the same discipline: don't stack volume, design the pipeline.

Three takeaways for builders:

1 — Indie has structural advantages at the model layer. Big lab models carry brand / API funnel / internal KPI obligations into every design decision. Q2_K at 4.5GB on an 8GB Mac is a SKU big labs can't ship — not because they can't build it, but because their business model won't let them.

2 — Data volume is not the lever. Pipeline design is. 10,000 verified examples + mistake recovery routing + source-audited reasoning outperformed the implicit assumption that "more tokens = better model."

3 — Stating your limits at ship time is method, not disclaimer. Test conditions, domain scope, distance from frontier — yuxinlu1 put all of it in the model card. That's how builder credibility compounds.

This continues a thread I've been running: orchestration > model across workflow / operator / org-ASI / protocol layers. yuxinlu1 adds one level above that: specialization > scale, even within the model layer itself.

Consumer tracks: "how many points did the benchmark go up this month?"
Builder asks: "what specific pain point is the big lab ignoring, and can I make it work on a Mac with 8GB?"

不必做全能。把一个具体问题做到好用。That's the indie winning move at the model layer.
